messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Hairdresser
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Photos): Related photos, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amir's life was forever altered on a sweltering summer day two years ago when he was rushed to the hospital with excruciating chest pain. The diagnosis – a severe case of pneumonia that had progressed to sepsis – left him fighting for his life. As a hairdresser, Amir was no stranger to high-pressure situations, but nothing could have prepared him for the trauma that awaited him in those sterile hospital corridors. The memory of that fateful day still lingered vividly in Amir's mind. He recalled the antiseptic smell wafting through the air as he lay helplessly on the hospital bed, the beeping of machines echoing in his ears, and the feeling of utter powerlessness that gripped him as the medical team frantically worked to stabilize his condition. Even now, whenever he caught a whiff of disinfectant, Amir was instantly transported back to those harrowing moments. As Amir slowly began to recover from his ordeal, he noticed that certain triggers would set off a chain reaction within him. Looking at photos taken during his hospital stay or undergoing routine medical check-ups would send his body into overdrive, leaving him tense and ready to react to any perceived danger. The aftermath of nightmares, too, left Amir reeling – the residue of fear and anxiety clinging to him like a shroud. What frightened Amir most was the constant threat he perceived within himself. His negative emotions – fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame – swirled together in a toxic brew that seemed impossible to contain. He felt as though his body was perpetually on high alert, ready to respond to any danger, real or imagined. Even the slightest provocation could trigger a physical reaction, leaving Amir feeling as though he was losing control. Amir's memories of his illness lingered, refusing to be exorcised. The smell of antiseptic would waft up, transporting him back to those hospital corridors, and he'd feel a searing pain in his chest – the same spot where the pneumonia had ravaged his body. Sometimes, Amir couldn't shake off the emotional intensity of that experience even when no clear image or memory presented itself. The aftermath of his trauma had left Amir with a crippling sense of distrust in his own body. He believed it was an enemy, perpetually reacting as if danger lurked around every corner, even when he knew he was safe. The fear that he might be "going crazy" due to his erratic reactions consumed him, eroding what little confidence remained. As the months dragged on, Amir's avoidance behaviors became more entrenched. He began to shy away from social engagements, unable to bear the thought of being around people while feeling so vulnerable. His work as a hairdresser suffered too – the proximity to chemicals and disinfectants proved too much for him to handle. The tension in his body was palpable, causing his hands to shake as he tried to style clients' hair. The final straw came when Amir's best friend, Rachel, staged an intervention, expressing her concern over his increasing isolation and erratic behavior. It was then that Amir realized he needed help – not just for himself but also for the relationships he cherished. He hoped that therapy would provide a safe space to untangle the web of emotions that had entangled him since his illness. As Amir sat in the therapist's office, he couldn't shake off the fear that lingered within him. What if he truly was losing his grip on reality? What if his body continued to betray him at every turn? The uncertainty hung over him like a specter, casting a shadow over his fragile hopes for recovery.
